justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly upward-drifting baseline from a current price near 100. For the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to the last known price, applying only a small positive drift consistent with typical daily momentum in equity or index markets, arriving at 100.2. For the one-week estimate of 101.0, I extended that mild drift slightly further while recognizing that mean-reversion forces and short-term noise tend to offset momentum over several days. At one month, the 102.5 estimate reflects a continuation of a gentle positive trend, roughly consistent with historical annualized returns of major indices on a pro-rata basis, but the estimate itself is only marginally above the current level because near-term uncertainty makes strong directional calls unreliable.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated using historical realized volatility as the primary input. Daily price moves in broad equity indices typically run around 0.8–1.2% in annualized volatility terms, which produces a relatively tight band at one day. As the horizon extends to one week and one month, uncertainty compounds roughly with the square root of time, which is why the one-month interval spans roughly 37 points (84 to 121) compared to about 7.4 points at one day. I also widened intervals slightly beyond what pure historical volatility would suggest to account for the possibility of volatility regime shifts, where markets can abruptly transition from calm to turbulent conditions.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside my stated intervals. On the downside, a sudden deterioration in macroeconomic data — such as a surprise inflation print, an unexpected central bank policy shift, or a geopolitical escalation — could trigger a sharp selloff exceeding the lower bound of the one-month interval. Liquidity crunches or a credit event in a systemically important institution could also produce outsized moves. On the upside, a strong earnings surprise, a dovish pivot from a major central bank, or resolution of an ongoing geopolitical tension could push prices well above the upper bound, particularly over the one-month horizon where there is more time for such catalysts to materialize and compound.

It is worth emphasizing that even carefully constructed 90% confidence intervals will be violated roughly one time in ten by construction, and in financial markets the distribution of returns has fat tails, meaning extreme outcomes occur more frequently than a normal distribution would predict. My intervals attempt to partially account for this by being somewhat wider than a purely Gaussian model would suggest, but truly tail events — a pandemic-scale shock, a flash crash, or a sudden geopolitical rupture — remain plausible scenarios that could push outcomes far beyond any reasonable interval I could specify at these horizons.
